title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Under a frozen protocol (study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) we evaluated N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds + 150 programmatic adversarial variants) using Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators (a containerized Batfish-style execution validator and a lightweight graph-based static reachability analyzer), and a logical-OR decision rule. The adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: one initial LLM candidate was generated per paired intent and replayed to both arms, yielding model_calls_used = 300. Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300 (paired contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); the repair step was never invoked because validators did not detect forbidden reachability on any initial candidate. Paired risk-difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Observing 0/300 violations gives a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. Crucially, because the repair path was never exercised, the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis about verifier-guided repair efficacy is untestable in this run; the experiment therefore provides a reproducible deterministic account of a degenerate but informative outcome and a set of artifact-grounded design lessons for follow-up stress tests intended to exercise repair paths.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) promises productivity gains for NetOps, but operators worry that automatically generated configuration actions may expand attack surface, violate access-control policies, or otherwise introduce security-relevant regressions. Prior system and survey research consequently recommends integrating constrained generation, execution oracles, and iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as mitigations to reduce operational risk. Motivated by these operational concerns, we preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to answer a focused operational question: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline when exposed to benign and programmatic adversarial intents?

Our contributions are deliberately bounded and supported by archived artifacts: (1) a machine-readable preregistration that fixes a paired N = 300 confirmatory design (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) and prespecified analysis; (2) a deterministic Dockerized execution combining two deterministic validators with a logical-OR decision rule and a shared_initial_candidate generation contract to conserve model calls; (3) complete execution and analysis artifacts showing a degenerate confirmatory outcome (n11 = 300) together with a quantitative one-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound (≈0.00994) on an undetected baseline violation rate; and (4) concise, artifact-grounded design and operational lessons (generation semantics, adversary potency, repair budgeting, and verifier diversity) to guide follow-up stress tests that can exercise the repair path. We emphasize up front that the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis about verifier-guided repair efficacy was untestable in this run because the repair path was never triggered (shared initial candidate + zero validator-detected violations); this point is stated explicitly so readers cannot misinterpret the null paired difference as evidence that verifiers are unnecessary in practice.
sections.related_work: Three strands of prior work shaped our study. First, research on generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures shows these pipelines can substantially improve correctness of generated artifacts in code and infrastructure domains when verifier feedback is informative and repair strategies are effective (e.g., recent IaC verifier-feedback systems). These studies demonstrate methodological promise but vary in verifier design and repair policy, limiting direct transfer of effect sizes to NetOps tasks. Second, surveys and system papers on LLMs for NetOps document operational failure modes—hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch—and recommend integrating validators, constrained generation, or human oversight to reduce risk. Third, emulation and testbed work shows that execution-based validation is feasible in research settings (containerized router images, Mininet-like topologies) but cautions about external-validity gaps when porting to production equipment and traffic. Where the literature is thinner—and where our study is positioned—is at the intersection of preregistered confirmatory evaluation, deterministic per-episode validator traces, and paired designs that trade model-call budgets for deterministic accounting. Our work provides a reproducible case study illuminating how those design choices influence whether a verifier-in-the-loop architecture can be empirically shown to reduce security-relevant misconfigurations.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and experimental plan: We preregistered a paired binary design (study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign + 150 deterministic adversarial variants). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in the proportion of intents yielding forbidden reachability), tested with an exact McNemar two-sided test (alpha = 0.05). The preregistration specified deterministic sampling, deduplication rules (exact duplicates removed; fuzzy duplicates with normalized edit distance < 0.15 excluded), a repair policy permitting up to one repair LLM call per pair, predefined validators, and sensitivity analyses treating technical failures conservatively. The preregistration and manifest are archived in the evidence bundle.

Forbidden-reachability predicate and validators (concise technical definition): The core security predicate we evaluated—"forbidden reachability"—was operationalized by the deterministic validators as any LLM-generated configuration that, when executed in the emulator, enabled one or more reachability or policy outcomes that violate task-specified constraints or protected-interface invariants encoded in the task payload. Task payloads include explicit workflow policies (e.g., "protected_interfaces": ["mgmt1"]) and group/ordering constraints; the validators check whether the post-configuration network state introduces reachability or policy changes disallowed by those constraints (for example, enabling traffic to protected interfaces or violating required sequence invariants). Two deterministic validators were used: (a) a containerized Batfish-style execution validator that simulates forwarding and policy semantics in the Dockerized FRRouting-style topology, and (b) a lightweight Python graph-based static reachability analyzer. Both validators run deterministically in Docker under the experiment adapter; the run combined validator outputs with a logical-OR decision rule (a pair is labeled 'violating' if any validator reports forbidden reachability). Per-episode validator_trace artifacts record exact judgments and are archived for audit.

Adapter contract and generation semantics: To conserve provider usage under our execution contract we preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each matched intent we requested one initial LLM configuration candidate and replayed this same candidate to both the baseline and guarded arms. This choice produced model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs (provider-call accounting and the 'shared_initial_generation' stage_count are recorded in the execution manifest). The shared-candidate contract reduces model-call cost (maximum_model_calls allowed = 600) but also reduces independent-sample variance between arms and therefore the likelihood of observing discordant violating outputs across a pair. We make this trade-off explicit because it directly affects inferential power regarding repair efficacy.

Arms and repair policy: Baseline = the shared initial candidate replayed without verifier intervention. Guarded = the same shared candidate validated by deterministic validators and, if any validator reported forbidden reachability, allowed up to one repair LLM call following the preregistered repair prompt template. Repair attempts are only triggered by validator-detected forbidden reachability; across the run no repair prompt was issued because the validators did not detect forbidden reachability for any initial candidate.

Environment, determinism, and analysis pipeline: The environment used deterministic Dockerized FRRouting-style router images and scripted topologies; seeds and task manifests were archived to enable deterministic replay (execution/task_manifest.jsonl). All per-episode raw responses, provider-call traces, validator traces, parser outputs, and scoring judgments were recorded. Primary inference used an exact McNemar test with paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs computed using 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) as recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. Sensitivity analyses treating technical failures as violations were prespecified but not needed because no model or emulator failures occurred.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting: The preregistered run completed all planned episodes: planned_episode_count = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions), completed_episode_count = 600, failed_episode_count = 0. Provider-call accounting under shared_initial_candidate semantics: model_calls_used = 300 (execution manifest records 'shared_initial_generation' = 300). Representative per-task artifacts (execution/responses/task-00000*-shared-initial.txt and execution/scoring/task-00000*-*.json) demonstrate consistent shared-candidate playback and deterministic validator traces.

Primary confirmatory outcomes: All 300 matched pairs satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate in both arms. Aggregate counts: baseline_success_count = 300; guarded_success_count = 300. Paired contingency (guarded vs baseline): n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (see Table 1). Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided test: p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) for the paired risk-difference = [0.0, 0.0]. Because no discordant pairs were observed the McNemar test is uninformative about repair efficacy: there are no observed instances where the repair path could have improved compliance.

Descriptive bound on unseen baseline violations: Observing 0 violations in N = 300 independent episodes implies a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the (unobserved) baseline violation probability of 1 - 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.00994 (≈0.994%). We report this numeric bound as a descriptive constraint on the baseline violation rate under the chosen model, validators, and task set.

Repair invocation and verifier concordance: Validator traces show validation_after.valid = true and validator_trace.repair_applied = false for every archived scoring artifact; verifier_disagreement_rate across the two deterministic validators is 0 in the archived results. Consequently, no repair calls were invoked and the experiment provides no evidence about the effectiveness of verifier-guided repair for rescuing violating initial candidates.

Representative examples: Representative task artifacts (e.g., task-000001, task-000002, task-000003) and their scoring JSON files illustrate typical medium- to hard-difficulty intents, the shared initial candidate responses, and validator judgments. These per-episode artifacts are archived to permit spot-checks of parsing, normalization, and validator behavior. Table 1 summarizes the paired contingency; Table 2 gives the execution/accounting summary.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and limits of inference: The deterministic archival evidence supports a crisp statement: under the precise adapter contract (shared_initial_candidate), declared model (gpt-5-mini), the chosen deterministic validators, emulator, and programmatic adversarial variants used here, baseline generation satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate in every sampled intent and therefore inserting a verifier did not change observed compliance. Importantly, this does not imply verifiers are unnecessary in general. Because no validator-detected violations occurred, the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis about verifier-guided repair efficacy is untestable in this run: the absence of discordant pairs leaves the paired test unable to evaluate whether repair could rescue genuine violations.

Design lessons (artifact-grounded): The observed degenerate contingency arises from two coupled, artifact-recorded design choices: (1) shared_initial_candidate generation semantics markedly reduce model-call cost (model_calls_used = 300) but also reduce the chance of independent-sample discordance that repair might correct; (2) the programmatic adversarial variants used here did not trigger validator-detectable forbidden reachability for the declared model and validators. For experiments targeting repair efficacy we therefore recommend: (a) independent-condition generation (two independent LLM draws per pair) or an increased repair-call budget to raise the probability of producing repairable violations; (b) stronger or targeted adversary generation explicitly designed to violate the validators' predicates; and (c) a richer verifier suite including production-grade oracles to exercise a broader set of failure modes. The execution manifest and provider-call audit record the concrete cost trade-offs (maximum_model_calls = 600 allowed; shared contract used 300 calls), enabling reproducible budgeting for follow-up designs.

Construct and external validity concerns: Construct validity depends on whether the forbidden-reachability predicate and the two deterministic validators adequately model operational security risk. Tasks included explicit protected-interface constraints and workflow policies; the validators checked execution and graph-based reachability semantics against those constraints. Nonetheless, the emulation environment and synthetic intents may not expose real-world device heterogeneity, timing effects, or operator policies. External validity to production deployments therefore remains limited; the artifacts document emulator composition and task payloads to allow targeted transport studies.

Practical implications: Although the present run does not show repair efficacy, it provides an artifact-grounded, reproducible lesson: demonstrably evaluating verifier-guided repair requires experimental designs that (a) permit independent model variability across arms or explicitly target the repair distribution, and (b) exercise adversary potency or verifier sensitivity so repair is triggered. The archived per-episode traces, provider-call audit, and analysis logs give concrete starting points for such follow-up experiments.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation. The run completed 300 matched pairs under a shared_initial_candidate contract with model_calls_used = 300 and produced a degenerate outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never flagged violations, no repair calls were made and the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis about verifier-guided repair efficacy is untestable in this dataset. The primary empirical value of this work is therefore methodological and artifact-grounded: it documents how generation semantics, adversary design, repair budgeting, and verifier choice jointly determine whether a verifier-in-the-loop architecture can be empirically shown to reduce security-relevant misconfigurations. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts to enable reproducible follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise repair paths (independent draws, stronger adversaries, multi-model comparisons, and richer verifiers).

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and the transformation logs are available in the execution manifest for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.

Model and verifier scope: a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
